title_en: Supplication, Seeking a Means of Approach, and Calling for Aid
body_ar:
أمر الله عباده أن يدعوه ووعدهم بالإجابة، وعلمهم الأسباب التي تجعل دعاءهم مستجاباً، ومنها التوسل إليه بأسمائه وصفاته وبالأعمال الصالحة ودعاء الصالحين، ولكن أدخل الناس في ذلك أموراً في التوسل بالأشخاص ونحو ذلك مما فيه خلاف، وأولى للمسلم اجتنابه لأنه قد يكون وسيلة إلى الشرك.
ذكر معنى الربوبية:
بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم الحمد لله رب العالمين، وأصلي وأسلم على من بعث رحمة للعالمين، وعلى آله وأصحابه ومن اهتدى بهديه واستن بسنته إلى يوم الدين. أما بعد: فيقول الشيخ حفظه الله تعالى: (وبالربوبية وحدوه فهو الذي تعنو له الوجوه) ......
تعريف الربوبية عند العرب:
هذا شروع في ذكر توحيد الربوبية، وهو على التقسيم الذي ذكرناه يُعَدُّ القسم الثالث من أقسام التوحيد، والمقصود به: إثبات الربوبية لله تعالى ونفيها عن كل ما عداه. والربوبية: مصدر صناعي من رَبَّ الشيء يَرُبُّهُ إذا كان مهيمناً عليه مسيطراً. والعرب تشتق من هذه المادة أربعة أفعال، فيقال: رَبَّهُ يَرُبُّهُ إذا استولى عليه...
body_en:
*[Site synopsis]* God commanded His servants to call upon Him and promised them that He would answer, and taught them the causes that make their supplication answered. Among these is seeking a means of approach to Him (tawassul) through His names and attributes, through righteous deeds, and through the supplication of the righteous. But people have brought into this matters concerning seeking a means of approach through persons and the like, over which there is disagreement; and it is preferable for the Muslim to avoid it, because it may be a means leading to associating partners with God (shirk).

## On the meaning of lordship

In the name of God, the All-Merciful, the Mercy-Giving. Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds. I ask God's blessing and peace upon the one sent as a mercy to the worlds, and upon his family and his Companions, and upon all who have taken guidance from his guidance and followed his practice until the Day of Judgement. To proceed: the Sheikh, may God preserve him, says: *(And by lordship declare Him one, for He is the one before whom faces humble themselves.)* ......

## What the Arabs understood by "lordship"

This is the beginning of the treatment of the oneness of God in His lordship (tawḥīd al-rubūbiyyah), which, on the division we have mentioned, is reckoned the third of the divisions of the oneness of God. What is meant by it is affirming lordship of God, exalted is He, and denying it of everything other than Him. "Rubūbiyyah" is an abstract noun formed from "rabba al-shayʾa yarubbuhu", said when one has command and mastery over a thing. The Arabs derive four verbs from this root: one says "rabbahu yarubbuhu" when he has taken possession of it …

flags.context: the record breaks off and the full text sits behind a download
options: render with an excerpt banner and link the .doc
flags.note: Excerpt only, style guide section 9. It breaks off on an ellipsis after the first of the four verbs the Sheikh announces he will derive, and long before any of the three subjects of the title — supplication, seeking a means of approach, and calling for aid — is reached. The complete text sits behind /medias/doc/L-30.doc. The English ends exactly where the Arabic ends and completes nothing. Must not be rendered as a whole lesson.

flags.arabic: الفقرة الافتتاحية مقابل ما بعد العنوان الفرعي
flags.context: the synopsis paragraph against the transcribed opening of the lesson
options: mark the synopsis as the site's own and the remainder as the Sheikh's words
present the whole record as the Sheikh's words
flags.note: The record has two authors. The first paragraph is a synopsis written by the site — it speaks about the lesson and its subject in the third person and does not begin with the opening formula. Everything from the section heading onward is transcribed speech in the Sheikh's own voice. The site must not present the synopsis as his words.

flags.context: the formula introducing each quoted line of the versified creed being commented on
options: read it as the author of the versified base text, distinct from the lecturer
read it as Sheikh al-Dedew quoting his own verse
flags.note: Getting this referent wrong would misattribute a creedal formulation, so it is flagged on every record in which the formula appears. These lessons are a commentary on a versified creed (nazm): the transcriber introduces each base-text line with 'the Sheikh, may God preserve him, said', and the commentary follows. 'حفظه الله' is used of the living, which at first sight fits Sheikh al-Dedew himself. Three passages inside the run settle it otherwise. Record 719 has the speaker giving thanks for 'completing the commentary on the Sheikh's versification' and describing what 'the Sheikh' chose to leave undetailed — a commentator does not ordinarily speak of his own base text that way while expounding it. Record 716 describes the base text as a versification of the Mukhtaṣar of Khalil ibn Ishaq by 'one of the scholars'. Record 718 introduces the same quoted lines with 'the versifier said'. The reading adopted throughout this slice is therefore that 'the Sheikh' is the living author of the versified base text and the lecturer is his commentator. The author is nowhere named, and the identification should be confirmed by the Sheikh's office before publication, because the bracketed verse and the prose around it carry different attributions.

flags.arabic: أموراً في التوسل بالأشخاص ونحو ذلك مما فيه خلاف، وأولى للمسلم اجتنابه لأنه قد يكون وسيلة إلى الشرك
flags.context: the site's synopsis, on seeking a means of approach through persons
options: it is preferable for the Muslim to avoid it
it is better for the Muslim to keep away from it
flags.note: The most consequential sentence in the record and the likeliest to be mistranslated. Three things must hold. First, the ruling: 'أولى … اجتنابه' is a statement of what is preferable, one step below even 'disliked (makrūh)' on the Maliki grading and nowhere near 'forbidden (ḥarām)'. Any English that reads as prohibition — 'should not', 'must avoid', 'is not allowed' — misstates it, and the style guide names this as a fixed error class. Second, the Sheikh expressly records that there is disagreement (خلاف) on the question and does not resolve it; the English lists the disagreement and does not resolve it either. Third, tawassul through persons is one of the most contested questions between Muslim currents and an English page on it will be read partisanly whatever it says, so style guide section 12 applies and the decision to publish belongs to Ummah Collective and the Sheikh's office. Note finally that the whole sentence sits in the site's synopsis: the transcribed lesson never reaches the question, so this cannot be presented as the Sheikh's considered position on it.

flags.context: the reason given in the site's synopsis
options: because it may be a means leading to associating partners with God
because it can lead to associating partners with God
because it is a means to associating partners with God
flags.note: 'قد يكون' is 'may be', not 'is'. The reasoning is that of blocking the means to harm (sadd al-dharāʾiʿ), the hallmark Maliki principle, and that principle works precisely on what may lead to a harm rather than on what does. Removing the 'may' would convert a precautionary argument into an accusation.

flags.arabic: يُعَدُّ القسم الثالث من أقسام التوحيد
flags.context: the transcribed portion, on where lordship falls among the divisions of tawḥīd
options: record the ordering as served and flag that its basis is outside the excerpt
flags.note: The Sheikh counts the oneness of God in His lordship as the THIRD division, referring back to 'the division we have mentioned', which is not in the served text. Most English-language treatments place lordship first. A reader who knows the common threefold scheme will think the text is in error; it is not, it is following a scheme set out in an earlier lesson that the excerpt does not contain. Rendered as served, and the basis of the ordering must not be guessed at.

flags.context: the quoted line of the versified creed
options: before whom faces are bowed low
flags.note: 'عنا يعنو' is to submit and be brought low; the line alludes to Sūrat Ṭā Hā 20:111, 'وعنت الوجوه للحي القيوم'. The allusion is not marked in the source and has not been marked in the English.

translator_notes: One of a run of fifteen records, IDs 707-721, in the written-creed section, all uploaded on 9 and 10 May 2011 within a few hours of one another, all built to the same template and all excerpts. Each carries a site-written synopsis, then a section heading, then the opening formula and the first lines of a lesson, and then breaks off on an ellipsis; the full text sits behind a .doc download in the /medias/doc/L-* series, numbered L-26 to L-39 in the same order as the IDs. The uniform timestamps are a bulk upload and say nothing about when the lesson was delivered.

The record contains two distinct voices and the English keeps them apart. The opening paragraph is a synopsis written by the site, about the lesson and in the third person; everything from the section heading onward is the Sheikh's own words as transcribed. Nothing in the synopsis may be quoted as his.

The source's final line, 'تحميل المادة' ('download the material'), is the label of a download link in the page furniture, not part of the text. It is recorded as source_download_link and omitted from body_ar and body_en.

The base text being commented on is identified inside this run. Record 719 has the Sheikh speaking of 'completing the commentary on the Sheikh's versification', and of that versifier's rendering of Khalil's Jāmiʿ in some five hundred lines; record 716 describes the base text as a versification of the Mukhtaṣar of Khalil ibn Ishaq whose opening section is on creed; and record 718 introduces the same quoted lines with 'the versifier said'. Taken together these settle that 'the Sheikh, may God preserve him' in this run is the living author of the versified base text and not the lecturer. The author is never named.
The record is broken twice: six dots stand where the commentary on the quoted verse should be, and the text breaks off again at the end. The three subjects of its title are never reached.

'مصدر صناعي' is the grammarians' term for a noun coined by suffixing -iyyah to make an abstract; rendered descriptively rather than transliterated, since the Sheikh is explaining the word's formation to students.
'الاستغاثة' in the title is rendered 'calling for aid' rather than 'seeking help', to keep it distinct from the ordinary seeking of help (istiʿānah) which is not at issue in the contested question.
No ruling term from the five-rulings table appears anywhere in the record. The one ruling word in the record, 'أولى', is a term of preference and is treated in its own flag.
